Upon such facts the learned Special Judge held that the Senior Special Judge having taken cognizance of the instant special case on 22.5.75 without there being any sanction to prosecute the accused respondent Abdur Rahim and without addressing the Government for obtaining requisite sanction for the prosecution of the case, there has been a non-compliance of the mandatory provisions of section 6(5) of the Criminal law Amendment Act, 1958. The Special Judge further held that the taking of cognizance on receipt of the complaint without prior sanction and without writing to the Government for such sanction is a contravention of the provisions of section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1958 and the taking of cognizance for prosecution of the accused Abdur Rahim as a public servant on 22.5.75 was illegal. The learned Special Judge relied upon the cases of Jahirul Huq Khan Vs. The State, 9 DLR (Dacca) 109,Md. Baharuddin Sarkar, Vs. The State10 DLR (Dacca) 321 and A.F.M. Taher Vs. The State 10 DLR (Dacca) 370, in support of his decision. Dr. Aleem Al-Razee, learned 

 “Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), or in any other law, the previous sanction of the appropriate Government shall be required for any prosecution under this Act and such sanction shall be sufficient for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence triable under this Act : Provided that no such sanction shall be required in respect of a case transferred under the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 4 or by virtue of sub-section (4) of that section" 

 It was held by Hamoodur Rahman J. (as his Lordship then was) sitting singly in the decision reported in 9 DLR (Dacca) 109 that the previous sanction of the appropriate Government is necessary to vest a Special Judge with jurisdiction in any case which has not stood automatically transferred to him under sub-section (4) of section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1954. In the opinion of the learned Judge, prosecution includes initiation or commencement of a criminal proceeding and begins when a formal charge is exhibited against the offenders. The learned Judge further held that without the sanction the special Judge has no jurisdiction either to take cognizance of the offence charged or to continue to take any proceeding in connection with that prosecution. It was further held that the absence of the sanction renders the entire prosecution void ab initio and this defect cannot be cured by obtaining a subsequent sanction during the pendency of the proceeding. 

 8. 23.9.58 the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1958 (Act XL of 1958) was enacted which repealed and re-enacted with certain amendments the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1948. The provision for obtaining previous sanction for the prosecution of a public servant before a Special Judge was made in section 6(5) of the new Act that is, Act XL of 1958, which was as follows : 

 6(5) “Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, or in any other law, previous sanction of the appropriate Government shall be required for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence under this Act and such sanction shall be sufficient for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence triable under this Act: 

 Provided that in cases where the complaint or report referred to in sub-section (1) of section 4 is not accompanied by such sanction the Special Judge shall, immediately on receipt of the complaint or report address by letter, the appropriate Government in the matter, and if the required sanction is neither received nor refused within sixty days of the receipt of the letter by the appropriate Government such sanction shall be deemed to have been duly accorded: 

 Explanation:-For the purpose of this sub-section, "appropriate Government" shall mean the Government which at the time of the commission of the offence was the appropriate Government. 

 9. The ratio decidendi of the cases reported in 9 DLR (Dacca) 109 and 10 DLR (Dacca) 321 and 370 is that when a complaint or report against a public servant is not accompanied by a sanction to prosecute a public servant, the Special Judge shall stay his hands if he takes any steps which can in Jaw be interpreted as taking cognizance of the case, the entire prosecution will be void ab initio. The first proviso to section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 has, in our opinion, effected a qualitative change in the position of law. If the complaint or report is not accompanied by a sanction the Special Judge is required to write to the Government immediately for such sanction. To write to the Government for such sanction is in our opinion, to take cognizance of the case or at least to take a proceeding in connection with the prosecution of the case. As such we think that those decisions which debar the Special Judge from taking cognizance at all without the previous sanction of the Government have lost their validity and relevance owing to the introduction of the first proviso to section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1958. 

 10. The necessity of receiving previous sanction from the Government for the prosecution of a civil servant is nothing new and the practice has its origin in section 197 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, which is as follows: 

 197 (1) "When any person who is a Judge within the meaning of section 19 of the Penal Code, or when any Magistrate, or when any public servant who is not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government, is accused of any offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, no Court shall take cognizance of such offence except with the previous sanction of the Government." 

 The prohibitive tenor in the language of the law needs to be noted. "No Court shall take cognizance of such offence except with the previous sanction of the Government." On the face of it the law seems to say, no sanction no cognizance. 

 11. Mr. Sohrab Ali, the learned Deputy Attorney General has cited the case of Dr. Mozammel Huq Chowdhury Vs. The Chief Martial Law Administrator, 32 DLR. (A.D.) 100, wherein the provisions of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure came up for consideration. It was argued before the Appellate Division that the sanction of the Government to prosecute a Public servant is a pre-condition before cognizance is taken by the court concerned. Repelling this contention the Appellate Division observed,this proposition is not tenable inasmuch as the language of section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not put any 'Such precondition to be fulfilled. Sanction can be obtained after submission of charge-sheet but before the trial commences. It may be noticed that whereas the language of section 197, Cr.P.C enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of such offence except with the previous sanction of the Government, section 6(51 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 merely provides that previous sanction of the Government shall be required for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence under this Act. If sanction can be obtained after submission of charge-sheet but before the trial commences in terms of the language of section 197 Cr.P.C., we do not see why the same interpretation cannot be made in respect of the sanction required under section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 especially when the language employed in the latter Act is much less prohibitive in tenor. 

 12. In the instant case the Senior Special Judge took cognizance on 22.5.75 and the necessary sanction was accorded on 29.5.75/31.5 75. Although the original sanction was found missing from the Court's records and an attested copy of the original sanction was marked Ext.10 at the time of trial, yet it cannot be said that the sanction was obtained after the charge was framed. The records show that the charge was framed on 22.9.75. Apparently the sanction was accorded before the charge was framed. We have therefore, no hesitation in holding that the learned Special Judge was mistaken in his finding that the trial was void ab initio. We find no defect in the sanction Ext.10 and we hold that the sanction was given in substantial compliance with the provisions of section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958. We hold that although the special Judge is required to write to the Government for sanction if on the date of receipt of the complaint or report the sanction is not available, yet the first proviso to section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1958 will be substantially complied with if the sanction to prosecute is accorded by the Government before the charge is framed, even if the Special Judge has failed to write to the appropriate authority for necessary sanction and has taken cognizance of the case without writing to the Government for sanction,
